title: Kings of the Court
text:
How It Works

1 — Data collection
Shot data comes from the NBA’s ShotChartDetail endpoint via nba_api. I loop through all 30 teams with player_id=0 (all players) and a 0.6 s sleep between requests to avoid rate limits. The full dataset is cached as a Parquet file.
from nba_api.stats.endpoints import shotchartdetail

resp = shotchartdetail.ShotChartDetail(
    team_id=team_id,
    player_id=0,
    season_nullable="2025-26",
    season_type_all_star="Regular Season",
    context_measure_simple="FGA",
)
df = resp.get_data_frames()[0]


2 — Zone assignment
Each shot is assigned a zone by a pure-geometry function using LOC_X and LOC_Y. Corner 3s are detected first (|x| ≥ 220, y ≤ 140), then above-the-break 3s (distance from rim ≥ 237.5), then paint zones by y-cutoff, then mid-range by side and height.


3 — Finding leaders
For each zone, shots are grouped by player, FG% is computed, and the player with the highest FG% above the minimum-attempts threshold is selected.


4 — Animation
The animation is built with matplotlib.animation.FuncAnimation. Each zone gets a 66-frame slot (~2.2 s at 30 fps):

Frames 0–7: zone highlights, player name and stats appear
Frames 8–29: Bézier arcs grow from shot location → basket
Frames 30–43: full arcs held visible
Frames 44–59: arcs retract basket → shot location
Frame 60: arcs fade, zone dims

The Bézier control point is placed 30% of the shot distance above the straight-line path, making the trajectory read clearly as traveling into the rim. The active zone is highlighted by a precomputed RGBA grid rendered with imshow.

title: NFL WR Injury Analysis
text:
Takeaways

At 5’9”, 164 lbs, Brennan Thompson is a genuine outlier — no comparable receiver appears in this sample of 170 notable NFL wideouts over the past decade.
Size alone does not predict season-ending injuries in this data: the distributions between injured and non-injured groups overlap heavily.
If anything, larger receivers show slightly higher injury rates when split at the median, which runs counter to the “fragile small receiver” narrative.
The more meaningful concern for Thompson may not be injury frequency but durability at the point of contact — a question this dataset can’t answer without play-type and contact data.

This is an exploratory, descriptive analysis. With ~170 players and no controls for position role, snap count, age, or playing style, these patterns are observational — not causal.

title: MLB Strikeout Predictor
text:
This tool predicts how many strikeouts a starting pitcher will record against a given opponent in an upcoming game. Select any active 2026 MLB starter and an opposing team — the model returns a predicted K count with a transparent breakdown of the key factors driving the estimate.
Model inputs:

K/9 — The pitcher’s season strikeout rate per nine innings (primary signal)
Whiff% / SwStr% — Swinging-strike rate, a pitch-quality proxy from Statcast
Opponent K% — How often the opposing lineup strikes out, relative to the league average
Projected IP — The pitcher’s average innings per start (scales the opportunity)

Prediction formula:
\[\hat{K} = \frac{K/9}{9} \times \overline{IP_{GS}} \times \frac{Opp\ K\%}{Lg\ K\%} \times f_{whiff}\]
Confidence range uses Poisson variance scaled by model uncertainty.
